sections.learningObjectives:
- Define common nervous and endocrine word parts, including roots for the brain, nerves, spinal cord, and endocrine glands and hormones.
- Build and decode medical terms for the nervous and endocrine systems using prefixes, combining forms, and suffixes.
- Recognize common neurological and endocrine conditions and procedures by their terminology.
- Apply correct terminology when documenting and communicating in the medical office, and escalate concerning symptoms to licensed staff.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Neur/o is the word-part that means 'nerve.' Nerves are the body's message wires that carry signals between the brain and the rest of the body.

### Question 2

Encephal/o means 'brain.' Encephalitis is like a 'brain fire' — swelling inside the brain itself, which is different from the protective coverings around it.

### Question 3

The cerebrum is the big 'thinking cap' of the brain. The word-part cerebr/o points to that big upper part where ideas and memories live.

### Question 4

Myel/o is the word-part for the spinal cord, and -gram means 'a picture or record.' So a myelogram is a picture of the spinal cord.

### Question 5

The meninges are like a padded, protective blanket wrapped around the brain and spinal cord. The word-part mening/o points to that blanket.

### Question 6

Nerve roots are where big nerves plug into the spinal cord, like roots of a tree. Radiculopathy means a nerve root is sick or squeezed, which can cause pain down an arm or leg.

### Question 7

Para- means the lower half. Paraplegia means the legs and lower body can't move. Hemi- is one side, quadri- is all four limbs, and mono- is just one limb.

### Question 8

Hemi- means 'half.' If someone has hemiplegia, one whole side of their body — an arm and a leg on the same side — cannot move.

### Question 9

Aphasia means the 'talking part' of the brain is hurt, so a person may have trouble finding words or understanding others — like a computer that can't load its language program.

### Question 10

An- means 'without.' Anesthesia means 'without feeling' — like when the dentist numbs your mouth so you don't feel anything.

### Question 11

Psych/o means 'mind.' A psychiatrist is a doctor who helps people when their mind or emotions are struggling.

### Question 12

The word-part -lepsy means 'seizure.' Epilepsy is a condition where a person's brain has repeated seizure storms, like a circuit that flickers on and off.

### Question 13

-oma means 'tumor.' An adenoma is a growth that starts in gland tissue, like a little bump in a gland such as the thyroid or pituitary.

### Question 14

Endocrine glands are like sprinklers that spray their chemicals straight into the river of blood, so the message travels all over the body. Exocrine glands use tubes (ducts) instead.

### Question 15

Crin/o means 'to secrete.' An endocrinologist is a doctor who is an expert on the body's hormone factories — like the thyroid and pancreas — and the chemicals they send out.

### Question 16

Hyper- means 'too much,' glyc/o is 'sugar,' and -emia is 'in the blood.' Hyperglycemia means too much sugar in the blood.

### Question 17

-uria means 'in the urine.' Glycosuria means sugar is spilling into the urine, like when a cup overflows because there is too much sugar in the blood.

### Question 18

Dips/o means 'thirst' and poly- means 'a lot.' Polydipsia means feeling thirsty all the time, like a mouth that never feels watered.

### Question 19

-uria is the word-part for 'urine,' and poly- means 'a lot.' Polyuria means going to the bathroom to pee way more than usual.

### Question 20

The adrenal glands are two little hats that sit on top of your kidneys and make 'get ready' hormones. The word-part adren/o points to them.

### Question 21

The thyroid is a butterfly-shaped gland in the front of your neck. The word-part thyr/o points to it.

### Question 22

Calc/o is 'calcium.' Hypercalcemia means too much calcium is floating in the blood, like adding too much of an ingredient to a recipe.

### Question 23

Insulin is like a key that unlocks your cells' doors so sugar can go inside and be used for energy. Without enough keys, sugar stays trapped in the blood.

### Question 24

Glucagon is insulin's opposite twin. When blood sugar gets too low, glucagon tells the liver to release stored sugar, like opening the pantry when the kitchen runs out.

### Question 25

The pituitary is like the boss of the hormone team. It sends out orders that tell other glands — like the thyroid and adrenal glands — when to work.

### Question 26

ADH is the body's 'save water' hormone. Without it, the kidneys don't hold onto water, so a person pees a lot and gets very thirsty — that's diabetes insipidus.

### Question 27

Thyroid hormones are like the gas pedal for your body's engine. More thyroid hormone makes the engine run faster and hotter; less makes it run slow.

### Question 28

Calcitonin is like a 'calcium saver' that helps tuck extra calcium back into your bones so there is less floating in the blood.

### Question 29

PTH is the 'calcium lifter.' When blood calcium dips too low, PTH asks the bones, kidneys, and gut to push more calcium into the blood.

### Question 30

The adrenal medulla is the 'alarm bell' of your body. When you're scared or excited, it squirts out epinephrine and norepinephrine to make your heart pound and your senses sharpen.

### Question 31

The adrenal gland has two layers. The outer layer, the cortex, makes cortisol (the 'long-term stress' hormone) and aldosterone (the 'salt and water' hormone).

### Question 32

Epinephrine is your body's 'super-speed' button. When something scary happens, it floods in and makes your heart race and your hands shake so you're ready to run or fight.

### Question 33

The pineal gland is a tiny clock inside your brain. It makes melatonin, the 'sleepy signal' that tells your body when it's time to wind down at night.

### Question 34

The pancreas is a two-in-one worker. One part squirts sugar-control hormones into the blood, and another part squirts digestive juices through tubes into the gut.

### Question 35

The thymus is like a school for immune cells. It trains special 'T cells' to recognize and fight off germs.

### Question 36

The gonads are the body's 'growth and baby-making' glands. Ovaries make the female hormones, and testes make the male hormone testosterone.

### Question 37

Oxytocin is the 'bonding and birth' hormone. It helps a mother's muscles squeeze during labor and helps milk flow when nursing a baby.

### Question 38

Growth hormone is the body's 'grow taller' signal. It tells your bones and muscles to get bigger as you grow up.

### Question 39

ACTH is like a phone call from the pituitary to the adrenal gland's outer layer saying, 'Make your stress hormone now!'

### Question 40

TSH is a 'start working' message from the pituitary to the thyroid, telling it to make its energy-setting hormones.

### Question 41

Neur/o is 'nerve' and -itis means 'swelling or irritation.' Neuritis is a nerve that has become irritated and inflamed.

### Question 42

-oma means 'a lump or tumor.' A neuroma is a growth that starts from nerve tissue, like a knot forming along a nerve.

### Question 43

-algia means 'pain.' Neuralgia is pain that travels along a nerve, like a sharp electrical zing following the nerve's path.

### Question 44

-pathy means 'disease.' Peripheral neuropathy means the nerves in the hands and feet are damaged, which can make them feel numb, tingly, or painful.

### Question 45

A cerebrovascular accident is what people call a stroke. It happens when a blood vessel to the brain gets blocked or bursts, so part of the brain suddenly stops getting its fuel.

### Question 46

A fever with a very stiff neck and bad headache can mean a dangerous swelling around the brain. The right move is to get help from a doctor or nurse right away, not to wait.

### Question 47

Think of the brain wrapped in a blanket. Meningitis is when the blanket (meninges) is inflamed; encephalitis is when the brain itself is inflamed.

### Question 48

Nerves are wrapped in a fatty coating called myelin, like the plastic coating on a wire. In multiple sclerosis, the body's defense system strips that coating, so messages get scrambled.

### Question 49

Dopamine is the brain's 'smooth movement' helper. In Parkinson disease, the cells that make dopamine fade away, so movements become shaky and stiff.

### Question 50

Alzheimer disease slowly makes it hard to remember things and think clearly, like a library where the books gradually get harder to find.

### Question 51

An EEG is like a weather map for the brain's electricity. It shows the brain's electrical waves to help doctors find unusual patterns like seizures.

### Question 52

A TIA is a 'warning tap on the shoulder.' For a few minutes, the brain's blood flow is briefly blocked, causing stroke symptoms that go away — but it's a serious warning sign.

### Question 53

Hydrocephalus means 'water in the head.' The brain makes a clear fluid to cushion itself, but if too much collects, it presses on the brain like an overfilled water balloon.

### Question 54

Ataxia means 'without coordination.' It's when the brain's balance-and-timing system is off, making movements clumsy or wobbly.

### Question 55

Dementia is when a person's thinking and memory fade enough that everyday tasks become hard, like a computer slowly losing files it needs to run.

### Question 56

In type 1 diabetes, the body's own defenses attack the insulin-making cells, so almost no insulin is left. The person needs insulin medicine to replace what's missing.

### Question 57

In type 2 diabetes, the body still makes insulin, but the cells stop listening to it — like having keys that no longer fit the locks, so sugar builds up in the blood.

### Question 58

Hyperglycemia is 'too much sugar in the blood.' It's like pouring too much sugar into a cup of tea — the blood gets overloaded.

### Question 59

When blood sugar drops too low, it's like a phone running out of battery — the body gets shaky, sweaty, and confused because its fuel is gone.

### Question 60

Glycosuria means sugar is showing up in the pee. Normally the kidneys keep sugar in the blood, but when there's too much, some spills over into the urine.

### Question 61

Hyperthyroidism is like a car engine revving too high — the body burns fuel too fast, so a person loses weight, feels jumpy, and their heart races.

### Question 62

Hypothyroidism is like an engine idling too low — everything runs slowly, so a person feels tired, gains weight, and gets cold easily.

### Question 63

A goiter is a swollen, enlarged thyroid gland in the neck, like the butterfly-shaped gland puffing up bigger than normal.

### Question 64

Cortisol is the body's 'long-term stress' hormone. Cushing syndrome happens when there's way too much of it, like a stress alarm that never turns off.

### Question 65

Addison disease is when the adrenal glands are too quiet and don't make enough cortisol, leaving a person tired with low blood pressure — the opposite of Cushing syndrome.

### Question 66

In acromegaly, too much growth hormone makes an adult's hands, feet, and face keep growing larger, like a photo being slowly stretched.

### Question 67

Natr/o is the word-part for sodium, which is the 'salt' mineral in your blood. Natr/o shows up in words about salt levels.

### Question 68

Kal/i is the secret code for potassium, a mineral that helps your heart and muscles work. Hypokalemia means too little potassium in the blood.

### Question 69

Phag/o means 'to eat,' and poly- means 'a lot.' Polyphagia means feeling hungry and eating way more than usual.

### Question 70

Gigantism happens when a child's body makes too much 'grow' hormone before they finish growing, so they become extremely tall. Acromegaly is the grown-up version where the hands and face get bigger.

### Question 71

A lumbar puncture is like drawing a small sample of the clear 'cushion fluid' that surrounds the brain and spinal cord, taken from the lower back so doctors can test it.

### Question 72

My/o means 'muscle.' An EMG is a test that listens to the tiny electrical signals muscles make, to see if the muscles and their nerves are working well.

### Question 73

Crani/o means 'skull' and -otomy means 'cutting into.' A craniotomy is when a surgeon carefully opens the skull, like opening a lid, to reach the brain.

### Question 74

TSH is like a report card for the thyroid. The pituitary sends more or less TSH depending on whether the thyroid is working too hard or too little, so doctors check it first.

### Question 75

For a fasting sugar test, the patient's 'tank' must be empty of food and drinks (except water) so the doctor can see the true resting sugar level.

### Question 76

The A1c test is like a three-month 'report card' for blood sugar. It shows how well sugar has been controlled over many weeks, not just one day.

### Question 77

-ectomy means 'cut out and remove.' A thyroidectomy is surgery to take out the butterfly-shaped gland in the neck.

### Question 78

Adren/o means 'adrenal gland' and -ectomy means 'remove.' An adrenalectomy is surgery to take out one of the little glands that sit on top of a kidney.

### Question 79

Two different problems share the word 'diabetes' because both make people pee a lot. Insipidus is a water-balance problem; mellitus is a sugar problem. Same nickname, different cause.

### Question 80

A pheochromocytoma is a rare growth in the 'alarm bell' part of the adrenal gland that leaks out too much 'rush' hormone, making blood pressure spike suddenly.

### Question 81

Thyroid storm is when an overactive thyroid suddenly 'overheats' the whole body, causing high fever and a racing heart. That's a fire alarm — you get help right away.

### Question 82

Myxedema is when the thyroid has been running far too low for a long time, making the body puffy, slow, and very tired — like a machine nearly out of power.

### Question 83

The thyroid is the one gland that loves iodine, using it to make its hormones. A radioactive iodine test tracks how much iodine the thyroid grabs, like a dye tracing its activity.

### Question 84

When a person with diabetes gets shaky, sweaty, and confused, their blood sugar may be dropping too low. The safe move is to get help from a nurse or doctor right away, not to wait.

### Question 85

FAST is a quick checklist for stroke: Face, Arm, Speech, and Time. If any of these are suddenly wrong, it's a 'call for help now' moment, because every minute counts.
